chunks: Besides that, we also have the distinction of prophethood among us, by virtue of which we subdued the strong and raised up the down-trodden.

When Allāh made Arabia enter (the fold of) His religion, and the people submitted to it willingly or unwillingly, you were among those who entered the religion either from greed or from fear, at a time when those who had gone first had preceded and the first muhājirūn had acquired their (peculiar) distinction.
ai.seo_question: How does Muawiya characterize the difference between the early companions and later converts in his letter to Ali?
ai.summary: Muawiya employs this rhetorical contrast to legitimize his political authority by framing the later mass conversions as opportunistic, thereby diminishing the spiritual merit of the general populace compared to the elite status of the Prophet's family and the earliest companions. This passage reflects the Umayyad narrative of *sabr* (patience) and political pragmatism, where entry into Islam was often viewed through the lens of tribal allegiance and power consolidation rather than pure devotion. The emphasis on 'desire or fear' underscores the tension between the *Ahl al-Bayt's* intrinsic spiritual precedence and the pragmatic, sometimes coerced, expansion of the Islamic state under the Umayyads.
